title: Conditionals: Real, Hypothetical, and Past
story_context: Marcus, a newer member of Ahmed's team, asks him for career advice after their shift. As they talk through real plans, hypothetical choices, and past regrets, Ahmed uses all three conditional types naturally — showing Marcus how English speakers reason about the future, imagine alternatives, and reflect on the past. By the end of the conversation, Marcus realizes he has just heard a grammar lesson without knowing it.
objectives: Form and use Type 1 conditionals for real or likely future situations
Form and use Type 2 conditionals for hypothetical or imaginary situations
Form and use Type 3 conditionals for counterfactual past situations
Distinguish which conditional type fits a given situation
target_phrases: If you apply early, you will have a better chance.
If I were in your position, I would start with a certificate program.
If he had asked for feedback, he would have improved faster.
Even if it's difficult, it will be worth it.
If I had known that earlier, I would have done things differently.
What would you do if you were offered a promotion?
If you study consistently, results will follow.

dialogue.title: Career Coaching with Conditionals
dialogue.context: Ahmed, now a supervisor, is mentoring Marcus — a newer warehouse associate who is unsure about his career path. All three conditional types arise naturally as they discuss real plans, hypothetical choices, and past regrets.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Ahmed, I've been thinking about my future here. If I stay in this position, will I ever move up?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Definitely. If you demonstrate strong performance consistently, management will notice. If you apply for the team lead position when it opens, you will have a real shot at it.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: But I don't have any supervisory experience yet.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: That's okay. If you volunteer to lead small projects now, you will build that experience before the role opens. Every step counts.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: What if I considered going back to school? Would that help?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Absolutely. If I were in your position, I would start with a certificate program — something in logistics or supply chain management. You could do it part-time.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: That sounds expensive. If I had more savings, I would enroll right now.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Check whether your employer offers tuition assistance. If the company provided support, would you enroll?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Yes, definitely! I didn't even know that was possible.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Many people don't. Honestly, if I had known about that program when I first arrived, I would have enrolled in my first year. I waited two years — that was time I could have used.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: A little. If I had asked my supervisor for advice earlier, he would have pointed me in the right direction sooner. But I've learned that regrets are just lessons. The important thing is what you do next.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: So to summarize — if I work hard now, I will get opportunities. If I had better resources, I would act faster. And if I had started earlier, I would have been further along by now.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Exactly. You've just summarized the three conditional types without even realizing it. That's progress.

pattern_drills.pattern: If + present simple, will + base verb. Use for real, likely, or possible future situations.
examples: If you apply early, you will have a better chance. (real plan — likely result)
If she studies every day, her English will improve quickly. (likely habit → likely outcome)
If the shipment arrives on time, we will meet the deadline. (real future condition)
If you volunteer for projects, management will notice your initiative. (action → natural consequence)
If you study consistently, results will follow. (general truth about real effort)
pattern_drills.your_turn: Say a real plan: 'If I [do something], I will [result].'

prompts.sentence: If you apply early, you ___ have a better chance. (Type 1 result)
If she ___ hard, her English will improve quickly. (Type 1 condition)
I ___ help you if you ask me. (Type 1 main clause)

pattern_drills.focus: Type 2 Conditionals — Hypothetical / Imaginary Present or Future
pattern_drills.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb. Use for imaginary, unlikely, or hypothetical situations. Use 'were' for all subjects (not 'was') in formal English.
examples: If I were in your position, I would start with a certificate program. (imagining yourself in another situation)
If he had more experience, he would apply for the promotion. (he doesn't have it — hypothetical)
If the company offered tuition support, I would enroll immediately. (imagining a condition that isn't currently true)
What would you do if you were offered a promotion? (hypothetical question)
If I were the manager, I would change the scheduling system. (clearly not the manager — imaginary)
pattern_drills.your_turn: Say: 'If I were in your position, I would start with a certificate program.'

prompts.sentence: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer. (use 'were' not 'was')
If he had more experience, he ___ apply for the role. (Type 2 result)
What ___ you do if you lost your job? (hypothetical question)

pattern_drills.focus: Type 3 Conditionals — Counterfactual Past (regrets and alternative histories)
pattern_drills.pattern: If + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle. Use to imagine how the past could have been different.
examples: If I had known about the program, I would have enrolled sooner. (I didn't know — imagining different past)
If he had asked for feedback, he would have improved faster. (he didn't ask — what could have happened)
If she had applied last year, she would have gotten the job. (she didn't apply — past regret)
If I had started saving earlier, I would have had enough money by now. (past action → different present)
If the team had communicated better, we would have avoided the problem. (past situation — counterfactual)
pattern_drills.your_turn: Say: 'If I had known about the program, I would have enrolled sooner.'

prompts.sentence: If I ___ known about it, I would have enrolled. (past perfect condition)
If she had applied, she would ___ gotten the job. (Type 3 result)
He would have finished on time if he ___ asked for help. (Type 3 condition)

pattern_drills.focus: Mixed Conditionals — Recognizing which type fits
pattern_drills.pattern: Read the situation and choose the correct conditional type. Real → Type 1. Hypothetical → Type 2. Counterfactual past → Type 3.
examples: The meeting is tomorrow. (real) → If you prepare tonight, you will feel more confident.
You are not the manager. (hypothetical) → If you were the manager, what would you change?
You didn't study last night. (past fact — regret) → If you had studied, you would have done better.
The company might offer a raise. (possible future) → If they offer a raise, I will accept immediately.
I didn't get the job last year. (past fact) → If I had applied earlier, I would have had more interviews.
pattern_drills.your_turn: Use all three types: a real plan, an imaginary situation, and a past regret.

prompts.sentence: Real plan (Type 1): If I practice every day, my English ___ improve.
Hypothetical (Type 2): If I ___ the manager, I would change the policy.
Past regret (Type 3): If she had studied, she ___ have passed.

listening_exercises.transcript: Marcus: 'Ahmed, if I study logistics part-time, will the company support me?' Ahmed: 'Absolutely. If you enroll and maintain good attendance, HR will approve tuition assistance. If you complete the certificate, you will qualify for the team lead position when it opens.' Marcus: 'And if I apply early, will I have a better chance?' Ahmed: 'Yes. If you submit your application in the first week, your chances improve significantly. I went through the same process — if you plan ahead, the opportunities are real.'
listening_exercises.question: Which type of conditional appears in Ahmed and Marcus's conversation?
options: Type 1 — real or likely future plans

listening_exercises.transcript: Director Kim: 'I noticed something in your self-evaluation, Ahmed. You wrote: «If I would have more experience, I would apply for the regional role.»' Ahmed: 'Is that wrong?' Director Kim: 'The idea is right, but the form is off. Don't put «would» in the if-part. Say «If I had more experience, I would apply.» The if-part uses past simple, not would.' Ahmed: 'So «If I would have...» is the mistake.' Director Kim: 'Exactly. That's the most common error. «If I had» — not «If I would have.»'
listening_exercises.question: What error did Ahmed make in his self-evaluation?
options: He used past perfect in the if-clause

listening_exercises.transcript: Ahmed: 'Marcus, I want to be honest with you. If I had asked my supervisor for career advice in my first year, I would have advanced faster. I waited two years — that's two years I can't get back.' Marcus: 'Do you regret it?' Ahmed: 'A little. But I've learned from it. If I were in your position right now, I would go to the HR office tomorrow and ask about the tuition program. And if you do that this week, you will have the paperwork ready before the deadline.' Marcus: 'So one is about the past, one is imaginary, and one is a real plan?' Ahmed: 'Exactly. You're already thinking about this the right way.'
listening_exercises.question: In Ahmed's advice, which conditional type does he use for his real recommendation to Marcus?
options: Type 3 — to discuss a past regret
Type 1 — a real plan with a likely result
He doesn't give a real recommendation

speaking_tasks.prompt: Talk about a real career goal using Type 1 conditionals (if + present, will). What will you do, and what results do you expect? Use at least 3 Type 1 conditionals. Record for 35 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: I have a clear plan for my career development. If I enroll in the logistics certificate program this fall, I will complete it within 18 months. If I earn that qualification, my chances of promotion will increase significantly. I also know that if I continue to build my supervisory skills in this role, management will trust me with more responsibility. And if I stay with this company for three more years and demonstrate consistent results, I will be in a strong position for a regional manager role. If you work with purpose, opportunities will follow — I genuinely believe that.
sentence_starters: If I [study / apply / practice] ..., I will ...
If I stay consistent with ..., the results will ...
One thing I know for certain: if I ..., I will ...

speaking_tasks.prompt: Use all three conditional types in one response. 1) What would you do differently if you could change your past? (Type 3). 2) What would you change about your current situation if you could? (Type 2). 3) What will you do starting now? (Type 1). Record for 40 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Let me reflect on all three. Looking back, if I had invested more time in studying English in my first year here, I would have advanced more quickly in my career — that's my biggest regret, and I won't let it define me. In terms of my current situation, if I had more free time each week, I would take a public speaking course, because I know that skill would open many doors. But I can't change the hours in a day. What I can control is what I do next: if I commit to 30 minutes of focused English practice every evening, my fluency will improve noticeably within six months. The past shaped me, the present situation constrains me, but the future is mine to build.
sentence_starters: Looking back, if I had ..., I would have ...
Right now, if I had more ..., I would ...
Going forward, if I ..., I will ...

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a career reflection (100-120 words) using all three conditional types. Include: one real plan (Type 1), one hypothetical situation (Type 2), and one past reflection (Type 3).
writing_tasks.example:
Reflecting on my career, I can see both past mistakes and future opportunities clearly.

Looking back, if I had taken a business communication course in my first year, I would have been promoted sooner. That early investment would have paid off enormously. It is a regret, but also a lesson.

In my current situation, if I had more financial flexibility, I would enroll in a degree program immediately and complete it as quickly as possible. The opportunity would transform my career trajectory.

However, I am focused on what I can control. If I develop my leadership skills consistently over the next two years, I will qualify for a senior management position. The path is clear — I just need to walk it with discipline and patience.
rubric: Include one conditional of each type: real future (Type 1), hypothetical present (Type 2), and past reflection (Type 3)
Use correct verb forms for each type — no 'would' in the if-clause
Connect ideas logically so the reflection tells a coherent story

writing_tasks.prompt: A friend is struggling at work and considering quitting. Write them a message (80-100 words) giving advice. Use all three conditional types: encourage them with Type 1, help them think hypothetically with Type 2, and acknowledge their past situation with Type 3.
writing_tasks.example:
Hi Lena,

I understand how frustrated you feel. If you had received better support from your manager in the beginning, your experience would have been very different — that wasn't your fault.

Before you decide, consider this: if you were to speak directly with HR about your concerns, what would you want them to know? That conversation might open doors.

And if you stay and address the issues systematically, your situation will improve — I've seen it happen. You are capable and hardworking.

Whatever you decide, I support you.

Ahmed
rubric: Open with empathy (acknowledge the friend's situation) before giving advice
Use at least one conditional of each type correctly
End with an encouraging, forward-looking statement

grammar_focus.title: Type 1: Real Conditional (Present → Future)
grammar_focus.explanation: Use Type 1 for real, possible, or likely situations. Structure: If + present simple, will + base verb. The if-clause can come first or second. You already use this structure whenever you discuss real plans — for example, 'If I finish early, I'll call you' is a natural Type 1 conditional you may have said many times.
examples: If you apply now, you will meet the deadline. (likely situation → likely result)
You will improve if you practice every day. (main clause first is also correct)
If it rains tomorrow, we will postpone the event.
If she studies hard, she will pass the exam.
Even if it's difficult, it will be worth the effort.

practice.sentence: If she ___ (apply) early, she ___ (have) more options.

grammar_focus.title: Type 2: Hypothetical Conditional (Imaginary Present/Future)
grammar_focus.explanation: Use Type 2 for imaginary, unlikely, or hypothetical situations. Structure: If + past simple, would + base verb. Use 'were' for all subjects in formal English. You already know 'I would approach this by...' and 'I would consider...' from job interview language in Unit 9 — the 'would' in those phrases comes from Type 2 conditional thinking.
examples: If I were you, I would accept the offer. ('were' not 'was' in formal English)
If he had more experience, he would apply for the role. (he doesn't — hypothetical)
If the company paid more, she would stay. (they don't — imagining otherwise)
What would you do if you lost your job? (hypothetical question)
If I could change one thing, I would improve our communication system.

practice.sentence: If I ___ (be) the manager, I ___ (change) this policy.
If she ___ (have) a car, she ___ (commute) faster.

grammar_focus.title: Type 3: Counterfactual Past (Imagining a Different Past)
grammar_focus.explanation: Use Type 3 for imagining how the past could have been different. Structure: If + past perfect (had + past participle), would have + past participle. Used to express regret, alternative histories, or past criticism.
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam. (I didn't study → I didn't pass)
If she had applied earlier, she would have gotten the job. (she didn't → she didn't get it)
If he had asked for help, he would have finished on time. (he didn't ask → he didn't finish)
I would have stayed if the conditions had been better. (main clause first is also possible)
If we had planned better, we would have avoided this problem.

practice.sentence: If I ___ (know) about the program, I ___ (enroll).
If they ___ (communicate) earlier, we ___ (avoid) the problem.

questions.question: Which conditional describes a real or likely future situation?
Choose the correct Type 1 conditional:
options: If I would study, I will pass.
If I study, I will pass.
If I had studied, I will pass.
If I study, I would pass.

questions.question: Choose the correct Type 2 conditional:
options: If I am rich, I buy a house.
If I were rich, I would buy a house.
If I had been rich, I would have bought a house.
If I will be rich, I buy a house.

questions.question: Choose the correct Type 3 conditional:
options: If I study, I will have passed.
If I studied, I would pass.
If I had studied, I would have passed.
If I would study, I had passed.

questions.question: In Type 2 conditionals, it is correct to say 'If I were you...' (using 'were' instead of 'was').
It is correct to say 'If I would have money, I would travel.' (using 'would' in the if-clause).
Type 1: If you ___ (practice) every day, your English ___ (improve).
Type 3: If she ___ (ask) for help, she ___ (finish) on time.
accept: had asked, she would have finished

questions.question: Match the conditional type to its use:
Marcus said 'If I had more savings, I would enroll.' This is a ___.
Find and fix the error: 'If I would know the answer, I would tell you.'
questions.correct: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
accept: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.

questions.question: Find and fix the error: 'If she had studied, she would passed the exam.'
questions.correct: If she had studied, she would have passed the exam.
accept: If she had studied, she would have passed the exam.

vocabulary.definition: imagined or supposed, not real — useful when discussing options or possibilities
vocabulary.example: Let's think about a hypothetical situation: what if the company offered you a promotion tomorrow?

vocabulary.definition: a different option or possibility that you could choose instead
vocabulary.example: If that plan doesn't work, we'll need a strong alternative.

vocabulary.definition: the final result or consequence of a situation or action
vocabulary.example: If you apply early, the outcome will likely be positive.

vocabulary.definition: to think carefully and honestly about something, especially the past
vocabulary.example: If I had reflected on my choices sooner, I would have changed direction earlier.

vocabulary.definition: a feeling of sadness about something that went wrong or was not done
vocabulary.example: If I had asked for help earlier, I would have fewer regrets about that year.

vocabulary.definition: a result that follows from an action or decision
vocabulary.example: If you miss the deadline, the consequence could be serious.
It's unlikely that he will get the job if he doesn't prepare.

vocabulary.definition: doing the same thing repeatedly and reliably over time
vocabulary.example: If you are consistent, your English will improve faster than you expect.

vocabulary.definition: the path or direction something takes as it develops over time
vocabulary.example: Your career trajectory depends on the choices you make in the next few years.

vocabulary.definition: to officially sign up for a course, program, or activity
vocabulary.example: If the company offers tuition support, I will enroll immediately.

cultural_notes: Americans frequently use all three conditional types in career counseling, job interviews, and performance reviews — fluency with conditionals signals professional language ability.
Type 2 conditionals with 'were' ('If I were you...', 'If she were here...') are standard in American formal and professional speech; 'was' is common in casual conversation.
In American workplace culture, managers often use conditionals when giving feedback: 'If you had communicated earlier, we would have avoided this problem' (Type 3 — showing accountability).
Conditional sentences are central to American negotiation language: 'If you could offer X, I would be willing to Y' is a standard negotiation structure.

Ahmed's use of Type 3 conditionals ('If I had known...') to reflect on his own career journey reflects the American value of self-reflection and continuous growth — acknowledging mistakes without being paralyzed by them.
